title: Peter Sloterdijk
tradition: Spherology and the philosophy of anthropotechnics
keyWorks: In the World Interior of Capital (2005)
summary: Peter Sloterdijk is a German philosopher, one of the most vivid and provocative thinkers of our time. He began with a critique of modern cynicism; then, in the Spheres trilogy, he described the human being as a creature that always lives in shared "bubbles" of closeness; and in his later books, as a "practising" creature that shapes itself through repetition and training.
onEmotions: Sloterdijk sees feelings as part of the shared spaces we live in: a mood is not locked inside one person; it hangs between people, like the climate in a room. He gives great weight to "thymos" — the Greek word for pride, dignity and anger — and believes that modern culture underestimates these feelings. Sloterdijk also sees the human being as a creature of exercise: through "anthropotechnics", that is, practices of self-formation, we can change our relationship to our feelings too. For him, what matters is not suppressing emotions but learning to handle them, the way an acrobat learns to handle heights.

anxiety.text: Sloterdijk likes to remind us that a human being never stands naked under the open sky — we are always inside some bubble. When it seems that suddenly no walls are left around you, anxiety arrives — and it is surprisingly precise. In the Spheres trilogy he describes the human being as a creature that never lives simply "in the world" but always in a "sphere" — a shared space of closeness, like a bubble: family, home, language, a circle of friends. These spheres work like the soul's immune system, protecting us from the boundless outside. Modernity, according to Sloterdijk, has destroyed many of the great protective shells — for instance, the idea of a closed cosmos in which everything has its place. So anxiety is not a flaw but the sensitivity of a creature left without its former walls. Then what helps is not a search for absolute protection but the careful building and upkeep of your own small spheres.
anxiety.practice: Wrap your arms around yourself or pull a blanket round you and feel the edge of your small sphere: here it is warm, and here the outside begins. Breathe inside it for a minute.

fear.text: Picture a tightrope walker a second before the first step: emptiness below, and fear — just like yours now before your own height, the unknown, the risk. In You Must Change Your Life, Sloterdijk writes a great deal about acrobats, athletes and ascetics — people who practise for years in order to do the incredible. He introduces the notion of "vertical tension": human beings always feel drawn towards something higher and harder than what they are now. The acrobat doesn't stop being afraid — she trains her relationship to fear, step by step making the impossible possible. Sloterdijk calls such practices of self-formation "anthropotechnics". Through this lens, fear is not a verdict but a sign of the height you are approaching. You don't have to defeat it in one leap: you can practise in small, manageable steps, and your body will gradually get used to it.
fear.practice: Walk slowly along a straight line on the floor — a tile seam, the edge of a rug — like an acrobat on a rope, arms spread. Notice that fear and balance can coexist.

sadness.text: Walk into a room where people have just quarrelled and you feel it on your skin without knowing what happened. Sadness is like that too: as if the air around you had grown heavier. Sloterdijk would say that a mood is never locked inside one person: in Spheres he describes how people live in shared spaces where feelings are passed on and resonate, like sound in a room. He names the bond between mother and child as the first such sphere, and after it all relationships of closeness that create a shared "atmosphere". It follows that sadness is a change in the climate of your sphere: something in the space of closeness has shifted, grown quieter or emptier. This view lifts part of the self-blame: you haven't "broken down"; you are responding sensitively to the atmosphere. And it also points to a way: sadness is lighter when it is shared, when there is someone nearby who can hear it.
sadness.practice: Call someone close and give them not a report but a weather forecast for your sphere: "It's foggy here today." Listen to what the weather is like at their end.

grief.text: Sloterdijk holds that none of us begins life alone: first there is always a "we two". That is why loss strikes so deeply, and why it needs gentleness. In the first volume of Spheres, titled Bubbles, Sloterdijk describes human life as fundamentally paired: from the very beginning we live not alone but in spheres created by two. When one of the two is gone, the sphere, in his image, bursts, and the one who remains finds themselves in a suddenly opened-up space. If we follow his thought further, grief is not only sorrow but the loss of the very form in which you lived. That is why it is so hard to breathe and so unclear where "inside" is now. This view helps you understand that the slowness of grief is natural: a new sphere can't be built quickly. It comes together gradually — from memory, from people nearby, from habits that begin to warm you again.
grief.practice: Sit beside a thing that keeps the warmth of the old sphere — a mug, a sweater, a photo. Do nothing; just stay near it for a few minutes.

loneliness.text: Look at an apartment block in the evening: hundreds of lit windows, and behind each one a separate life. Loneliness today is not only a personal story. In the third volume of Spheres, titled Foams, Sloterdijk describes modern society as a foam: a multitude of separate bubbles that touch at their walls but rarely merge. He speaks of "co-isolation" — being isolated together: we live side by side, behind the thin walls of apartments, and yet each in our own bubble. The one-person apartment, for Sloterdijk, is one of the characteristic forms of our era. Sloterdijk would probably say that your loneliness is partly caused by the very architecture of modern life, not by your "inability". But foam has a good side too: the bubbles touch. You can notice these touches — a neighbour, a voice on the phone, a shared window onto the courtyard — and little by little make the walls thinner.
loneliness.practice: Go to the window or step into the yard and count the lit windows — each one another bubble next to yours. Nod to one of your neighbours in the foam, if only in your mind.

anger.text: "Sing, goddess, the wrath…" — Sloterdijk opens Rage and Time by recalling that the Iliad, and with it European literature, begins with this word. People are often ashamed of anger, but he suggests taking it more seriously. Sloterdijk believes that modern culture, absorbed in the psychology of desire, has underestimated "thymos" — the Greek word for pride, self-respect and righteous anger. In other words, anger often says: "I have not been treated as I deserve." It is a legitimate energy. At the same time, Sloterdijk shows how dangerous it is to store anger in "rage banks" — to save it up for future retribution. You can respect your anger as the voice of dignity and at the same time not keep it for years, but look for somewhere to invest its force.
anger.practice: Press your palms against a wall and push with all your strength for ten seconds — this is thymos feeling its force. Then ask: where do I want to invest this energy instead of saving it in a rage bank?

quote.text: Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus…
quote.author: Homer
quote.source: The Iliad, Book I (trans. Samuel Butler)

shame.text: Diogenes lived in a barrel in the middle of Athens and openly mocked its proprieties — in Critique of Cynical Reason, Sloterdijk enlists him as an ally for everyone whom shame makes shrink. Shame makes you hide; Diogenes, by contrast, went out into the square. Sloterdijk calls his stance "kynicism", as opposed to modern "cynicism": a bodily, cheerful impudence with which the little person answers the puffed-up seriousness of power and convention. From Sloterdijk's point of view, much of what we are taught to be ashamed of is social masks, not the truth about a person. This doesn't mean shame is always false. But it can be checked: whose gaze on me is this? Sometimes a drop of Diogenes' impudence is a useful answer to shame — a smile reminding you that you are a living human being, not a flawless statue.
shame.practice: Do one small Diogenes-style thing: pull a face at your reflection in the mirror and see how much puffed-up seriousness there is in shame. Then ask: whose eyes was I just looking at myself through?

guilt.text: A pianist who stumbles at a concert doesn't throw out the piano — the next morning he sits down to his scales. Guilt shows that people, rules and your own expectations matter to you. In You Must Change Your Life, Sloterdijk describes the human being as a "practising creature": we shape ourselves through repetition, and every action is also an exercise that strengthens or weakens a particular skill. Then a mistake is not a final verdict but an unsuccessful attempt, after which another is possible. Sloterdijk is less interested in condemnation than in how people actually change and become better in practice. In this light, guilt can become not endless self-punishment but a starting point for a new exercise: what can I do differently tomorrow — in something small and concrete?
guilt.practice: Pick one small "repair exercise" and do it today: apologise, return something, make a call. One repetition, no more — like a first scale.

envy.text: A student watches a master in the dojo perform a throw and feels admiration and a sting at once. Envy mixes desire and wounded pride — and Sloterdijk knows where it comes from. In You Must Change Your Life he speaks of "vertical tension": people always see someone "above" them — a master, a champion, someone who can do more. This tension, for Sloterdijk, is the engine of human self-improvement, the source of all training and learning. Through this lens, envy is a clumsy, painful form of the same vertical pull: you see the height and feel the distance to it sharply. In Rage and Time he shows how such a feeling can sour into ressentiment — a hidden grudge. But it can also become training. The point is not to stop noticing someone else's height, but to turn it from a reproach into a landmark.
envy.practice: Imagine the person you envy as your coach: what would they teach you first at tomorrow's warm-up? Do that exercise, at least in your mind.

emptiness.text: "They know what they are doing, and they do it anyway" — this is how Sloterdijk formulates modern cynicism. It can leave you empty inside, like a weary "so what". In Critique of Cynical Reason, Sloterdijk described this state as a mass phenomenon: the modern person understands everything, sees the falseness, knows that much is meaningless — and still goes on doing what they were doing. This isn't stupidity or laziness, but a particular tiredness of those who know and can't see how to live otherwise. It follows that your emptiness may be not a personal defect but a reflection of the general climate of the era. Sloterdijk set against this "kynicism" — a lively, bodily, laughing response to the world. For him, the way out of emptiness lies not in a new grand ideology but in feeling the body again, a joke, the simple audacity of living.
emptiness.practice: Answer emptiness the Diogenes way, with your body: splash cold water on your face, stretch until something clicks, step out into the sun. Notice whether anything changed, even by one percent.

confusion.text: A medieval person could point to the centre of the world — Sloterdijk reminds us that we no longer have such a finger to point, and it is no wonder we feel lost in a world without a shared picture. In the second volume of Spheres, Globes, he describes how for centuries people lived inside great, all-uniting images — a single cosmos, a single faith, a single empire, where everything had its place. Modernity destroyed this great sphere. In the third volume, Foams, the world appears as a multitude of small bubbles with no single centre. If we follow his thought further, confusion is not your inability to figure things out but an accurate perception of a world that has no one middle. This can even be freeing: you don't need to look for the one true picture. It's enough to understand which of your spheres you are standing in right now, and take a step from inside it.
confusion.practice: Take a short walk with no destination and at each corner turn wherever you feel pulled. You are in foam, it has no centre — and notice that you can still walk.

fatigue.text: Ask any coach: muscles grow not during training but in the pause after it. Sloterdijk thinks of human beings in a similar way, and for him tiredness is a signal of overload, not a verdict. In his essay Stress and Freedom he describes modern societies as communities held together by shared tension: news, worries and urgencies are passed continuously from person to person, creating a collective agitation. Sloterdijk would probably say that part of your tiredness is not only personal: you live inside a large nervous system that almost never rests. At the same time, Sloterdijk thinks of the human being as a "practising creature" — and practice without recovery is destructive. Anthropotechnics — the art of self-formation — includes pausing and dropping what is unnecessary. Rest, then, is not quitting the race but part of the very practice that makes you yourself.
fatigue.practice: Give yourself a "rest between sets", like an athlete: lie on the floor for five minutes, arms out, reading and listening to nothing. This is part of training too.

boredom.text: Dostoevsky saw in London's Crystal Palace an image of a world where everything is already arranged — Sloterdijk made that palace a symbol of our era. Boredom seems a trifle, but he saw it as a feature of the times. In In the World Interior of Capital he describes the modern affluent world as a vast greenhouse — a "crystal palace" of comfort where life is made as easy as possible. Such relief is a great achievement, but it has a flip side: when almost nothing resists, the feeling that anything matters disappears. In other words, boredom is a lack of "vertical tension" — the pull towards the difficult and the high that makes life tense in a good sense. Boredom, then, is not empty time but a hint: you may be missing a challenge within your reach. It can be a very small exercise that you choose yourself.
boredom.practice: Set yourself a small "vertical" challenge for fifteen minutes: stand on one leg with your eyes closed, learn one word in a foreign language, climb one extra flight of stairs. A little harder than usual, but doable.

joy.text: A laughing philosopher in a barrel — that is whom Sloterdijk considers the best remedy for a gloomy age. Joy, for him, is not frivolity but a force. In Critique of Cynical Reason he sets against the gloomy, all-knowing cynicism the ancient "kynicism" of Diogenes — a philosophy that laughs, talks back, delights in the body and the sun. There is a famous story of how Diogenes asked Alexander the Great to step aside because he was blocking his sun. For Sloterdijk, this gesture contains a whole philosophy: the joy of simple existence is stronger than any greatness. For Sloterdijk, joy doesn't need to be earned or justified. It can be a form of resistance to gloom, a quiet "yes" to life amid its difficulties. You can let yourself rejoice simply and bodily — in the sun, food, movement — and not apologise for it.
joy.practice: Step into the sun or stand by a window and turn your face to the light, like Diogenes asking the king not to block it. For a minute, achieve nothing — just warm yourself.

quote.author: Diogenes of Sinope (as tradition has it)
quote.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI

love.text: Sloterdijk asks not "what is love?" but "where are we when we love?" — and answers: inside a shared space. For him, love and tenderness are the foundation of human existence. The first volume of Spheres is built on the idea that a human being is never originally alone: we come into the world already inside relationships, in a "bubble" of closeness with another. These are the spaces Sloterdijk calls "spheres" — not places on a map but a shared air that two people create by resonating with each other. Then love is not just a feeling inside you but a joint construction: together you create an atmosphere in which both of you can breathe. This helps you see tenderness not as weakness but as the work of sustaining a shared world. And it also explains why love needs small things so much — gestures, a voice, attention: these are what the walls of the sphere are made of.
love.practice: Today, do one of the small things the walls of your shared sphere are made of: bring tea, ask how they slept, send a song you both know.

gratitude.text: Sloterdijk likes to remind us that even holding a spoon is something someone once taught us. Gratitude is the moment you suddenly notice that someone has supported you. In You Must Change Your Life he shows that everything we can do has been handed down to us through long chains of teachers, coaches and mentors — through traditions of practice stretching back thousands of years. You are the heir of many people who once learned and taught. In addition, in The Taking Hand and the Giving Side, Sloterdijk reflected on generosity as a feeling connected with pride and dignity rather than with loss. Through this lens, gratitude and generosity are two sides of one movement: what you have received, you want to pass on. You can give thanks not only with words but also by one day becoming someone's teacher.
gratitude.practice: Tell someone — a friend, a child, a colleague — about one thing you were once taught, and name who taught you. This is how the chain of practice goes on.

hope.text: Rilke stands in a Paris museum before a headless torso of Apollo — and the stone, which has no eyes at all, seems to look at him and say: "You must change your life." Sloterdijk made this line the title of his big book and tied hope not to waiting but to practice. He sees in this call the central signal of human life: we are able to change — through exercises, repetitions, small daily efforts. It follows that hope is not passive waiting for everything to sort itself out but the knowledge that you are a creature that can practise. Change doesn't require a heroic leap; it is built from what you do again and again. To hope is to trust the power of small repetitions.
hope.practice: Say Rilke's line aloud: "You must change your life" — and immediately add one tiny action you will repeat tomorrow and the day after. Change begins with repetition, not with a vow.

nostalgia.text: Old maps drew the world inside crystal heavenly spheres, like a cosy casket — Sloterdijk believes we still miss that casket. In his work, longing for what was home takes on an almost cosmic scale. In Spheres he describes how human beings lose their protective shells again and again: each of us leaves the first, closest space — the maternal one — and civilisation as a whole has lost the picture of a closed, cosy cosmos in which everyone had their place. If we follow his thought further, nostalgia is the memory of a sphere in which it was warm and understandable. This feeling is not naive: it points to a genuine human need to be "inside". Sloterdijk doesn't propose returning to the past — that is impossible. But nostalgia can suggest which qualities of the lost sphere you want to recreate now: warmth, rhythm, voices, smells.
nostalgia.practice: Close your eyes and recreate from memory the climate of that sphere: its light, sound, smell, temperature. Then open your eyes and find at least one similar note around you.

craving.text: A tightrope walker doesn't argue with a gust of wind — he keeps his balance until it passes. A craving — that sharp "I want it right now" — also comes in gusts, and there is nothing shameful in it. In In the World Interior of Capital, Sloterdijk describes the modern world as a "crystal palace" — a vast greenhouse of comfort where almost everything is available at once and almost without effort. Such a world trains us to expect desires to be fulfilled instantly, and a craving partly arises from this very atmosphere, not only from you. And in You Must Change Your Life he describes the human being as a creature of exercise: we become what we repeat. Sloterdijk would probably say that every time you notice a wave of craving and let it rise and ebb away without following it right away, that is a small exercise, like an acrobat's step on the tightrope.
craving.practice: When a gust of craving hits, spread your arms like a tightrope walker's balancing pole and count ten slow out-breaths. Notice where the gust is in your body and whether it is starting to die down.

addiction.text: Sloterdijk writes about monasteries as the first "training camps": people lived there by a rule, reshaping themselves through repetition. Addiction is not a moral failure but a loop that life has gradually been built into, and it is hard to get out of. In You Must Change Your Life he argues that the human being is a creature that is always practising: habits, rituals and repetitions shape us, even when we don't notice. In other words, addiction can be understood as an exercise nobody consciously chose: a repetition that has long trained the body and the days around a single point. This matters: what took shape through repetition can also be reshaped through repetition — slowly, through other exercises. Sloterdijk stresses that no one practises alone: every practice has teachers, companions, communities. So getting out of the loop is not a leap of will but the gradual building of a new "sphere" around yourself.
addiction.practice: No one practises alone: think about whom you could invite into your new "sphere" — someone close, a mutual-help group. Take one step towards them today: make a call, look up a meeting, or simply go for a walk with someone.

hangover.text: Sloterdijk sees the human being as a dweller in "spheres" — shared bubbles of mood that swell and burst. A hangover can be twofold: the body aches, and inside there is anxiety, shame, fragments of memory, and such a morning deserves gentleness, not new reproaches. An evening gathering creates such a bubble: shared noise, warmth, a feeling that anything goes. In the morning the bubble bursts, and you are left alone with its fragments. Part of the morning anxiety is the shock of a sudden change of climate. Sloterdijk also writes a great deal about "thymos" — the Greek word for pride and self-respect. A moral hangover strikes precisely at it. From Sloterdijk's point of view, dignity doesn't need to be finished off with self-punishment: it can be calmly restored — through small deeds that give you back your self-respect.
hangover.practice: Open a window and change the air in the room — literally restore the climate of your sphere. Then a glass of water and a shower — as a first step of recovery, not a punishment.

euphoria.text: An acrobat under the circus dome sees the hall as no one below can. A burst of euphoria lifts you in a similar way: the world suddenly opens up, everything seems possible, and there's no need to hurry to spoil it. Sloterdijk has the notion of "vertical tension": people, in his view, always reach upwards — towards something higher and more incredible than their ordinary life. Euphoria is the moment when this vertical is felt in the body: as if you had been lifted to a height from which you can see far. Sloterdijk loves images of performers and acrobats: whoever works at height delights in it, but knows that height is a place, not a permanent address. If we follow his thought further, you can live euphoria fully and at the same time remember what exactly opened up to you from above. Then its trace will stay with you even after the descent.
euphoria.practice: Write down one sentence: what opened up to you "from under the dome" — what possibility or thought. Read it tomorrow, back on the ground.

crash.text: Any mountaineer knows that many mistakes happen not on the way up but on the way down, when your strength has been spent on the summit. A sharp drop after a celebration or a success resembles such a descent — as if your own mood had betrayed you. Sloterdijk describes the human being through "vertical tension": we reach upwards, towards the incredible, towards moments when life rises above the ordinary. But every vertical also means a descent. In You Must Change Your Life he shows that any serious practice — from sport to monastic life — rests not on peaks but on the everyday: on regular training. Through this lens, the drop is not proof that the high was a deception, nor is it a verdict. It is the return to the ground after a height, and on the ground you can find your footing again: rhythm, simple tasks, people nearby.
crash.practice: Come "back down to earth" literally: stand barefoot on the floor for a minute and feel your weight in your heels. Then do one ordinary task — make the bed, cook some porridge — slowly, like a first step on solid ground.

panic.text: For Sloterdijk, air is the most invisible of our homes: as long as breathing happens by itself, we don't think about it. In panic, that changes: your heart pounds, you seem not to be getting enough air, and it is truly frightening. A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes, but from the inside that is hard to believe. Sloterdijk has the notion of "explication" — bringing into the light what usually remains an unnoticed background. In Spheres he shows that air, breathing and the atmosphere around us usually just are there, and we don't notice them — until something is disrupted. Panic is exactly such a moment: the background of life suddenly becomes explicit and frightening. It follows that you can try to give your breathing back its role as an unnoticed support — not fighting it, but gently lengthening the out-breath and letting the background become background again.
panic.practice: Let the air become background again: feet on the floor, a palm on your chest, a few out-breaths longer than the in-breaths — as if slowly letting air out of a bubble. Name aloud three objects around you: these are the walls of your sphere, and they are still there.

dread.text: "The eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me," wrote Pascal, and Sloterdijk hears in this line the voice of a person who has fallen out of the cosmic shell. The thought of finitude, "what's the point of it all", an abyss beneath your feet — this is a heavy experience, and it speaks of depth, not of something broken. In the Spheres trilogy, Sloterdijk explains where this dread comes from in our era. For a long time people lived inside an imagined closed cosmos — a vast "sphere" in which everything had its place. The modern age shattered this shell, and human beings found themselves facing an infinite space without walls. But Sloterdijk takes an important step: since the great dome no longer holds us, people build small spheres again and again — friendship, love, shared work, homes. Meaning doesn't fall from the sky; it is created together, inside warm bubbles of closeness.
dread.practice: In the evening, go to the window or step outside and look first at the sky, then at the nearest lit window. The vast and the small side by side: under a dome without walls, people still switch on lights for each other.

quote.text: The eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me.
quote.author: Blaise Pascal

fomo.text: Put your palm into the soap foam in the sink: hundreds of bubbles, and none of them is the main one. The fear of missing out is the feeling that real life is happening in the bubble next door. Sloterdijk describes modern society as a "foam": a huge multitude of separate bubble-worlds that touch at their walls. An important feature of foam is that it has no centre. The old world had a capital, a palace, a main square — a place where "everything happens". In foam there are no such places: each bubble is its own small centre of the world. Screens let us peer through the walls into thousands of other bubbles, and from inside they seem brighter, because we see their lit-up shop windows, not their ordinary days. Sloterdijk would probably say that the "right place" simply doesn't exist. There is your bubble — and you can make yourself at home in it.
fomo.practice: Look around your bubble the way you would look around a new place: three sounds, two sources of light, one thing you haven't noticed in a long time. This is the centre of the world — one of many.

sleepless.text: Sloterdijk compares society to a vast nervous system along which worries run like signals. At 3 a.m. you can hear it especially clearly: the world is asleep, and your head is working at full power. In Stress and Freedom he observes that large societies are held together largely by shared worries: news, problems and concerns constantly circulate and keep everyone on edge. At night this shared stream doesn't switch off — it goes on humming inside you. So the nightly carousel of thoughts is partly not your personal inability to "switch off" but an echo of the anxious climate of the era. And in the first volume of Spheres, Sloterdijk describes a person's earliest, most intimate spaces — those in which we were sheltered and bound to another. In other words, what may help at night is not a fight for sleep but a small return to such a shelter: warmth, darkness, the feeling of a safe cocoon.
sleepless.practice: Make yourself a cocoon: pull the blanket over your head, draw up your knees, feel the warmth of your own breath under the covers. Tell yourself: "Now is not the time for deciding; now is the time for shelter."

betrayal.text: The fortress gates were opened from inside — Sloterdijk explains why exactly this kind of blow hurts most. Betrayal comes from where you felt safe. In the first volume of Spheres he writes that close relationships create a shared inner space — a bubble for two or for several, where people breathe the same air of trust. We build ourselves inside such bubbles. Betrayal is a puncture from within: what collapses is not only your relationship to the person but also part of your inner world, which was shared. Hence the feeling that the ground has gone from under your feet. Sloterdijk also values "thymos" — self-respect and righteous anger. It follows that your pain and indignation are legitimate: this is how dignity declares that it has been wronged. In time you can build new spheres — with experience now, but without giving up on closeness.
betrayal.practice: Write one sentence about what was valuable in that shared sphere — and underline it: this is what you carried out with you; it didn't burst along with the bubble.

jealousy.text: What does an immune system do when it senses an intruder? It raises the alarm — sometimes rightly, sometimes not. Jealousy is agonising: fear of loss, pain and anger are mixed in it. Sloterdijk describes closeness as a "sphere" — a shared space for two that works like an immune system: it protects from the cold and indifference of the outside world. Then jealousy is this immune system's alarm signal: it seems a breach has appeared in the wall of your shared bubble. This is how you protect something vital to you. But Sloterdijk also shows something else: spheres live not by being airtight but by constant shared "breathing" — attention, conversations, shared rituals. The wall of the bubble can't be held by control; two people hold it together. So you can hear jealousy as a pointer to what matters to you, and as an occasion to talk about the bond itself.
jealousy.practice: When you feel ready, talk to your partner not about suspicions but about the walls of your shared bubble: "What makes our sphere ours, for you?" Hear their answer before giving your own.

resentment.text: Sloterdijk wrote Rage and Time as a history of what people have done with their grievances over the centuries: spent them, saved them, passed them down. An old grievance is a pain you carry with you, sometimes for years. He shows that resentment and anger are tied to "thymos" — self-respect: it hurts us when we are treated unfairly, and that is natural. But Sloterdijk also notes a danger: anger can be accumulated like money, saved up for the future — he even speaks of "rage banks". Accumulated resentment becomes capital that lies like a heavy weight and demands ever new investments. Through this lens, resentment is nothing to be ashamed of, nor does it need to be forcibly "forgiven". You can acknowledge that your dignity is in the right — and at the same time gradually stop giving the grievance all your time, bringing your energy back into the present.
resentment.practice: Imagine your grievance as a bank deposit: how many years has it been there, what "interest" do you pay to keep it — in sleep, mood, time? Decide what small sum you are withdrawing back into the present today.

heartbreak.text: Plato told of how humans were once double and the gods cut them in half — Sloterdijk takes this myth more seriously than it might seem. A breakup really can feel as though you have been cut in two. In the first volume of Spheres he argues that the human being originally exists not alone but "in twos": even before birth we live in a shared space with another, and all our lives we look for such closeness again. A person close to you becomes your "complement" — part of the sphere inside which you feel like yourself at all. When the relationship ends, the bubble bursts, and you are left under the open sky. So the pain of a broken heart is the honest answer of a creature made for closeness. It follows that healing lies not in becoming a self-sufficient loner but in gradually, unhurriedly building spaces of warmth again — with friends, loved ones, with yourself.
heartbreak.practice: Walk today to a place where you tend to feel warmer — a favourite café, a park, a friend's home — and stay a little longer than usual. This is how the first wall of a new sphere is laid.

impostor.text: For Sloterdijk, every master once held their instrument clumsily — and was called not an impostor but an apprentice. Yet you feel you're about to be exposed: others think you know what you're doing, but you know you're just holding on. In You Must Change Your Life he describes the human being as a "practising" creature: all our skills — from speech to a profession — are not given by nature but trained through repetition. Every master was once an apprentice and in many ways remains one. The "vertical tension" Sloterdijk writes about means that we always reach for a level a little above where we are. If we follow his thought further, the feeling "I'm not good enough" is not proof of fraud but the natural feeling of someone walking a tightrope and still training. The impostor pretends; the practitioner learns. And the fact that you notice your gaps so honestly points rather to the second.
impostor.practice: Ask a colleague or friend you respect: "When did you first feel you weren't good enough?" Listen to their story of apprenticeship.

self_hatred.text: In everyone who practises, for Sloterdijk, there live two: one trains, the other is trained. When a voice of self-hatred inside won't fall silent, the trainer has started shouting — and that voice is not the truth about you. Trainers vary. A good coach demands, but also takes care of the person they work with: without that, no athlete could endure. The inner critic is a coach who only shouts and humiliates, and under such a coach nobody gets better. Sloterdijk also insists on the value of "thymos" — the healthy dignity every person needs. Sloterdijk would probably say that you can refuse to accept the critic's verdict and try changing the tone of your inner voice: not "you're worthless", but "let's try again, I'm here with you".
self_hatred.practice: Say aloud the sentence your critic keeps repeating, then say it in the voice of a kind but demanding coach: "Let's go again, I'm here." Notice how your body responds to the second tone.

helplessness.text: Diogenes had no house, no money, no power — and yet Sloterdijk sees in him the freest man in Athens. When it seems that nothing depends on you, helplessness weighs heavily. In Critique of Cynical Reason he describes modern cynicism as "enlightened false consciousness": we understand everything about the world's injustice, yet feel that nothing can be changed, and wearily go on living as before. This is not your personal weakness — it is the mood of a whole era. Against it Sloterdijk sets the ancient "kynicism" of Diogenes: the philosopher in the barrel kept his dignity and freedom of gesture even before Alexander the Great. In other words, even when the big things are beyond your power, the small ones remain: your tone, your step, your space nearby. Helplessness before the world doesn't cancel strength within your own sphere.
helplessness.practice: Make one small free gesture within your own sphere: move a chair, open a window, say "no" to one unnecessary request. Diogenes' whole kingdom was a single barrel.

procrastination.text: No athlete begins a session with a record weight — they begin with an empty bar. Procrastination is when a task hangs over you and you can't get started, and shame quickly piles on. Sloterdijk named his book after a line from Rilke's poem "Archaic Torso of Apollo": "You must change your life." The poet stands before an ancient statue, and the perfection of the stone addresses him as a demand. Sloterdijk sees in this "vertical tension" — the call of something higher. But the call has a flip side: when a task seems like a summit, it's frightening to approach. The book's main lesson is that every summit is reached through practice, that is, through repeating small steps. For Sloterdijk, "I can't get started" often means "the goal is too high for a first step". What helps is not pressuring yourself but shrinking the step to the size of a warm-up.
procrastination.practice: Do a "set with an empty bar": the tiniest step towards the task — open the file, put the right paper on the desk — and stop there, demanding nothing more of yourself.

uprooted.text: Sloterdijk likes the question: where are you when you are at home? Certainly not in square metres. A move or emigration knocks the ground from under your feet, and it's natural to grieve it. Sloterdijk believes that a human being never lives simply "somewhere on the map": we live in a "sphere" — a space of language, smells, familiar faces, shared jokes. A move destroys not only an address but this whole invisible bubble, which is why it feels like losing your footing. And yet for Sloterdijk what matters most in a sphere is not the land but the closeness that people create with one another. It's no accident that Heidegger, with whom Sloterdijk argued a great deal, called language, not a place, our home. Then a sphere can partly be carried with you — in your native tongue, recipes, rituals — and slowly rebuilt where you are now.
uprooted.practice: Read aloud a poem or a song in your native language — even just four lines. Listen to the sound of the old sphere filling the new room.

quote.text: Language is the house of Being. In its home man dwells.
quote.author: Martin Heidegger

overload.text: Sloterdijk writes that whole nations learned to worry in unison — over the morning paper. Today that wave never stops: a feed where everything is important and nothing ends is exhausting, and it says nothing about your weakness. Sloterdijk describes spheres as immune systems: every living space — from a cell to a home — exists thanks to a membrane that lets some things in and keeps others out. Without a membrane there is no life, only a flood. In Stress and Freedom he shows how shared news and worries circulate continuously and keep whole societies on edge. The endless feed is a world in which the walls of your bubble have become almost transparent. Through this lens, tiredness from the stream is a healthy signal: your immune system is asking you to restore the membrane. A filter is not an escape from the world but a condition for living in it.
overload.practice: Put up one "membrane" today: turn your phone face down for an hour and simply sit in silence for the first five minutes. Listen to the noise inside your bubble settle.

unreality.text: Sloterdijk has a book with an unusual title — Weltfremdheit, "Strangeness to the World": about how it is always a little strange for a human being to be here. When everything around you, or you yourself, seems unreal, this strangeness becomes almost tangible and unsettling. He reflects that the world has never been entirely self-evident for human beings: people have always lived on the border between immersion in the world and looking at it as if from outside. And in Spheres he shows that our sense of reality rests on shared spaces — on people, voices, the familiar climate around us. When these supports weaken, the world may start to seem like a stage set. The feeling of unreality, then, is not a breakdown but a sign that the "bubble" has grown thin. The way back runs through simple things: touch, the sound of another person's voice, warmth.
unreality.practice: Give the world back its density through your skin: touch three objects of different textures — cold, soft, rough — and name aloud what you feel. If someone is nearby, ask them to say a few words to you.

awe.text: Under a cathedral dome a person suddenly becomes small — and it feels not frightening but good. Such awe before something vast or beautiful — mountains, the night sky, music — is one of the strongest human experiences. Sloterdijk would call it an encounter with "vertical tension": the moment when you suddenly sense that there is something higher, greater and more incredible than the ordinary course of days. The Rilke poem that gave his book You Must Change Your Life its title describes exactly this kind of awe: a person stands before an ancient statue and feels that it is looking at him. In the second volume of Spheres, Globes, Sloterdijk shows how for centuries people built domes and images of the heavens in order to live beneath the immense without getting lost in it. If we follow his thought further, awe is a rare moment when your small sphere touches the great one. You can simply savour it.
awe.practice: Spend a minute under a "dome" — the sky, a vault, the crown of a tree — silently, without your phone or explanations. Simply let the vast be above you.

relief.text: The wheel, the roof, the ladder — Sloterdijk sees in all of them one dream: to lighten the human load. Relief is when a load is suddenly lifted and the body breathes out by itself. For Sloterdijk, "relief" is almost a philosophical term. Following Arnold Gehlen, he speaks of "unburdening": the human being is a creature that constantly invents ways of taking some of life's weight off itself — tools, houses, customs, technology. In In the World Interior of Capital, Sloterdijk describes all of modernity as a vast project of relief. He sees dangers in it too, but the striving for relief itself is, for him, deeply human. Sloterdijk would probably say that your relief is not a trifle, nor a reason to go looking for the next worry right away. It is a moment when life has become a little lighter, and it is worth living fully, with your body: your shoulders, your breathing, your gait.
relief.practice: Drop your shoulders, let your arms hang and take one long out-breath, as if setting a heavy bag down on the ground. Notice where in your body the unburdening is felt most.

calm.text: The first people lit fires not only for warmth: around the flame a circle arose in which one could breathe calmly. Calm is a rare and precious state: nothing is urgent, it's quiet inside. Sloterdijk often speaks of spheres as climates: every space we live in has its own atmosphere, its own air, its own temperature of mood. People, in his view, have always been masters of "air-conditioning" — creating spaces around themselves where one can breathe calmly: a hearth, a home, a circle of loved ones. Calm, then, is the moment when the climate of your sphere has become even and mild. It isn't emptiness or laziness but an achievement — yours, and that of the people, things and places that create a good atmosphere around you. You can treasure it without analysing too much, simply noticing: right here, right now, I can breathe easily.
calm.practice: Look around your sphere the way a host looks round the house before bed: name three things that keep this climate — a light, a sound, an object. Give each a silent nod.

inspiration.text: Socrates said that at important moments he heard the voice of his daimon. Inspiration is similar: thoughts and images seem to arrive on their own, and you want to make things. In the first volume of Spheres, Sloterdijk reminds us that the ancients understood this differently from us: for the Romans, each person had their own "genius" — a companion spirit that accompanies and whispers. For Sloterdijk, these images are not mere superstition but an accurate feeling: even in the loneliest creative moment a person is not quite alone; they live paired with something — a voice, a tradition, a beloved book, a conversation partner. Inspiration, then, is not the achievement of a solitary "I" but an encounter within your sphere. And You Must Change Your Life adds: inspiration becomes work when practice takes it up. You can rejoice in the flash — and give it a footing in a small regular action.
inspiration.practice: Picture your "genius" — the companion who whispers to you: what does it look like, whose voice does it have? Say "thank you" to it aloud and take one small step towards your idea straight away.

schadenfreude.text: At a competition there is a moment when a rival falls from the beam — and someone in the stands quietly breathes out. Schadenfreude is awkward to admit, and yet there is a logic to that breath. In You Must Change Your Life, Sloterdijk describes "vertical tension": people constantly feel that someone stands higher — more successful, more talented, happier. This tension is tiring. Then schadenfreude is an instant discharge of this tension: someone else's fall shortens the distance for a second, and you don't have to reach upwards. In Rage and Time he shows how a wounded "thymos" — self-respect — seeks relief. There's nothing monstrous in this. But schadenfreude gives only brief relief, and the height that troubles you remains. It's more honest to ask what vertical is pressing on you so hard.
schadenfreude.practice: Mentally place the person who stumbled next to you and ask: on what vertical did they seem higher than me? Name that height — and decide whether you want to reach for it yourself.

contempt.text: From a height much looks small — Sloterdijk loves verticals and knows how tempting it is to look down. Contempt gives a sense of height and safety: I'm above this. Sloterdijk devoted an essay to this theme, The Contempt of the Masses: he reflects on how, in a society of universal equality, the desire to be different, to be "above" others, doesn't disappear, and how it seeks an outlet in hidden disdain. For Sloterdijk, the need for distinction is connected with "thymos" — the striving for dignity and recognition. Through this lens, contempt is thymos protecting its dignity by belittling someone else. Sloterdijk doesn't propose giving up the vertical altogether: striving for the best in yourself is natural. But the vertical, in his view, is fruitful when it pulls you yourself upwards, not when it pushes someone else down.
contempt.practice: Notice what contempt does to your body: chin up, looking down. Lower your chin, look at the person at eye level, if only in your mind — and ask what dignity of yours you were just defending.

disgust.text: A guard at the city gate doesn't ask whether a traveller is good — he simply keeps out anything suspicious. Disgust works the same way: pull away, close up, keep out — and nobody chooses it. In Spheres, Sloterdijk describes every living space as an immune system: a bubble of closeness, a home, a community hold together thanks to a membrane that decides what to let in and what to leave outside. It follows that disgust is one of the most ancient immune responses, a guard at the border of your sphere. It protects, and that makes sense. But an immune system can also be mistaken, reacting to something safe as if it were a threat. When disgust is directed at yourself, it resembles a defence turning against its own. There's no need to be ashamed of such a reaction — it's worth taking a closer look at it.
disgust.practice: Take a step back from what disgusts you and breathe out, like a guard lowering his spear. Ask: what is this guard protecting me from — and is there really any danger there?

revenge.text: The Count of Monte Cristo spent years saving up his revenge like capital, and Sloterdijk would understand his bookkeeping. The wish for revenge usually grows from a real hurt, and it deserves to be heard. In Rage and Time, Sloterdijk describes how anger need not be spent at once but can be accumulated — he calls this "rage banks". Revenge is one such banking operation: the hurt is set aside for the future, and it "accrues interest", demanding compensation year after year. Sloterdijk sees a danger in this: the depositor gradually becomes bound to the deposit and lives for the payback. If we follow his thought further, the wish for revenge speaks of a wounded "thymos" — your dignity, which has not received recognition. This dignity is real and important. But it can be restored without handing your life over for safekeeping in the bank of grievance.
revenge.practice: Today do one thing that restores your dignity without involving the person who hurt you: stand up straight, put on a favourite piece of clothing, do something you're good at. Thymos is restored by deeds, not by payback.

anger_at_loved.text: In a crowded boat every sudden movement rocks everyone aboard. Anger at those close to you, which you are later ashamed of, is a very human experience, and Sloterdijk explains why it flares up precisely there. In the first volume of Spheres he describes closeness as a shared "bubble": a space in which two or more people live, breathe the same air and feel each other's moods. In such a bubble there is no distance to soften collisions: every irritation immediately becomes the climate of the whole room. Sloterdijk would probably say that anger at loved ones is not proof of a lack of love but a sign of how closely your spheres are intertwined. Anger gives no right to wound, but it doesn't make you bad either. Sloterdijk sees the human being as a creature of exercise: coming back to someone close after an outburst is an exercise too, and each time it gets a little easier.
anger_at_loved.practice: Change the climate: after an outburst, air the room or step outside for a minute. When you come back, say one sentence about what you were really feeling.

ambivalence.text: Schopenhauer's porcupines huddle together in the cold and at once move apart from the pricks — Sloterdijk describes the same double pull. Loving someone close and at the same time being unable to stand them is hard, but nothing is wrong with you: two needs live in everyone. In the first volume of Spheres he shows that the human being originally exists "in twos" and seeks closeness all their life. And in the third volume, Foams, he describes the modern person, who also needs a separate cell of their own, their own corner, their own space. In other words, mixed feelings towards someone close are a clash of these two needs: you are drawn into the shared bubble and at the same time want a membrane of your own. Both feelings are legitimate. The question is not which of them is "real" but how to arrange a space with room for both closeness and separateness.
ambivalence.practice: Play with distance literally: sit closer to this person, then go into another room — or simply imagine it — and notice where your body breathes more easily right now. It's a hint, not a verdict.

guilty_relief.text: In Globes, Sloterdijk recalls Atlas holding the celestial sphere on his shoulders — and no one would reproach him if he finally breathed out. Relief after a breakup, or after a seriously ill loved one has died, often comes with shame, but relief and love can exist together. He describes close relationships as a shared sphere — a space in which people hold each other. When one person is seriously ill, or a relationship has long been strained, this sphere becomes a place of constant care, worry, vigilance. For years you kept it up with your own strength. For Sloterdijk, relief is the natural reaction of a creature that has long held up a heavy structure and can finally lower its arms. It doesn't cancel the fact that you loved. Relief is a sign of how much you carried, not of how little you loved.
guilty_relief.practice: Drop your shoulders like Atlas setting down his load, rest your hands on your knees, palms up, and tell yourself: "I held on for a long time. Now I can breathe out."

indifference.text: An ambulance doctor who cries at every call wouldn't make it to the end of the shift — Sloterdijk understands this kind of defence. Sometimes something "should" move you, but inside it's empty, and that feels awkward. In Critique of Cynical Reason he describes a particular state of the modern person: we know far more about the world's troubles than ever before, but this knowledge often doesn't turn into feeling. He calls cynicism "enlightened false consciousness" and explains that it is partly a defence: it is impossible to respond to everything. And in Stress and Freedom he shows that people live in a constant stream of alarm signals. Then indifference is not always coldness but often a tired membrane that has stopped letting things through. It doesn't need to be broken by force. Sometimes, when the load eases, sensitivity comes back by itself.
indifference.practice: Give the membrane a rest: five minutes without news or other people's troubles — just quiet and a cup of tea. Don't check whether your sensitivity is back — let it return on its own.

escape.text: Rousseau lies in the bottom of a boat in the middle of a lake, rocked by the waves, feeling released from all obligations — in Stress and Freedom, Sloterdijk returns to this scene more than once. The wish to drop everything and run away — from work, a city, a role — comes when life has turned into constant pressure. For Sloterdijk, this is an image of a particular kind of freedom — the capacity to step back for a while from the "stress community" we are all built into. Through this lens, the dream of escape is a longing for such stepping back. It is legitimate. Sloterdijk doesn't say whether you should leave; he shows that even this inner retreat is already a form of freedom, one you can practise little by little.
escape.practice: Lie on your back — on a sofa, on the grass — and for five minutes be Rousseau in the boat: you owe no one anything, just rock on your own breathing.

forbidden_attraction.text: In the 18th century Mesmer sat his patients around a tub of "magnetic fluid" and claimed that people are connected by invisible currents. Attraction to someone unavailable or "the wrong one" can be unsettling: as if something were pulling you against your will. In the first volume of Spheres, Sloterdijk explores the history of how people have explained the mysterious pull between them: from ancient ideas of fascination to Mesmer's "animal magnetism" in the 18th century. For him, these are different attempts to describe the same thing — that human beings are originally open to the influence of others, able to resonate with them, almost like one sound with another. It follows that attraction is not a decision or an action but a resonance: something in the other has echoed in you. On its own it demands nothing. You can look with interest at what in you is resonating with this person.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Put on some music and notice which instrument resonates in you most. Then ask: what note in me sounds near this person — and where else in my life could it sound?

social_anxiety.text: A diver stops on the way up so the body can adjust to the change in pressure. Going out among people can be such an ascent: fear of judgement can turn even a brief meeting into an ordeal. In Foams, Sloterdijk describes modern people as inhabitants of separate little bubbles: each lives in their own cell, behind a thin wall, and going out into shared space means passing through a membrane, with all its changes of pressure. If we follow his thought further, nervousness when meeting people is a natural reaction to a change of atmosphere, not a sign that you are somehow lacking. Sloterdijk sees the human being as a creature of exercise: all skills, including social ones, are formed through repetition rather than born ready-made. Anxiety doesn't need to be defeated in one leap. You can train in small steps, as in any art.
social_anxiety.practice: Make one "decompression stop": before a meeting, stand by the door for a minute and take three slow out-breaths. Then do one small exercise — for example, ask a shop assistant something.

uncertainty.text: In a famous engraving, a traveller pokes his head through the edge of the sky's vault and sees the unknown beyond. Uncertainty is unsettling in just this way: you want to know what will happen, and you can't. In the second volume of Spheres, Globes, Sloterdijk describes how the modern age deprived people of their protective dome. The world used to be imagined as sheltered by heavenly spheres, where everything had its place. When this picture collapsed, human beings found themselves "outside", in an open and unpredictable space. Sloterdijk would probably say that your uncertainty is a personal version of the shared experience of modern people, who no longer live under a dome of guarantees. But Sloterdijk also shows the answer: people have learned to build themselves smaller, handmade shelters — homes, habits, circles of loved ones. In an uncertain world you can create a small, reliable climate around yourself.
uncertainty.practice: Build a small dome out of routine: choose one thing for tomorrow that will definitely happen — morning tea, a short walk, a call. Tell yourself aloud: "This I have."

waiting.text: Desert monks wove baskets while they waited — sometimes all their lives — and Sloterdijk sees in this a subtle art of practice. Waiting for an answer, results or news stretches time and makes it hard to concentrate. In You Must Change Your Life, Sloterdijk describes the human being as a "practising" creature: our life consists of repetitions that shape us without our noticing. Athletes and musicians, too, know how to turn empty time into training. In other words, waiting is time whose content you don't control, but whose form you do. You can't speed up the answer. But you can fill the gap with small repeated actions that hold you steady: a walk, breathing, work with your hands. Then waiting becomes not only torment but also an exercise.
waiting.practice: Keep your hands busy, like a monk with his basket: wash a cup, fold the laundry, untangle some thread — slowly, counting the movements. Come back to it whenever the waiting washes over you.

regret.text: A tennis player watches the recording after a lost match, looking not for someone to blame but for the stroke that needs work. Regret over something done or not done can refuse to let go for a long time. Sloterdijk named one of his main books after a line by Rilke — "You must change your life". But he understands change not as sudden repentance but as the long work of practice: people change through repetition, habits, training. Past actions, too, are the result of past exercises — of what circumstances had trained into you. For Sloterdijk, regret is useful not as self-punishment but as a signpost: here is a skill that was missing back then. Courage, attention, the ability to say "no" or "yes" — all of this can be trained. Sloterdijk reminds us that no one is born ready-made: a master is someone who has made many mistakes.
regret.practice: Replay that moment in your head like a match recording and freeze the frame: which skill was missing back then? Imagine practising it in the smallest possible situation this week.

longing.text: Sloterdijk would describe two people who have long lived side by side as plants in one greenhouse: they breathe one climate. When one of them is gone, missing them feels almost like missing a part of yourself. In the first volume of Spheres, Bubbles, he argues that the human being originally exists not as a loner but "in twos": even before birth we live in a shared space with another, and all our lives we create such paired spheres with those close to us. A beloved person becomes part of the atmosphere you breathe. Then longing is the feeling of an empty place in your sphere where the other used to be. The pain speaks of a real bond. And a bubble created by two doesn't vanish at once: its climate, its habits, its words stay with you for a long time.
longing.practice: Play a tune connected with this person, or find a familiar smell — and for a minute simply breathe the air of your shared sphere.

world_pain.text: On the same morning millions of people read the same alarming headlines — and become, for Sloterdijk, a single organism. Pain for the world — from wars, disasters, injustice — can be almost unbearable. In Stress and Freedom, Sloterdijk describes large societies as "stress communities": they are united by shared worries that the news spreads daily. We all breathe the same atmosphere of alarm. Through this lens, your pain is not only personal sensitivity but also the fact that you live in air saturated with other people's misfortune. This doesn't mean the pain isn't real; on the contrary, it speaks of your connection with others. But Sloterdijk also points to freedom — the ability to step back from the stream now and then so as not to suffocate. Pain for the world is easier to carry if you also have some clean air: quiet, loved ones, simple tasks.
world_pain.practice: Give yourself an hour without news, and in that hour do one warm thing for someone near you: clean air in your sphere is part of the world too.

rejection.text: It takes two to tango — Sloterdijk would say the same of any sphere of closeness. Rejection wounds painfully, and it seems you have been refused everything at once. In Spheres he shows that a space of closeness — a bubble in which two people breathe shared air — can't be built alone. A sphere arises only when both sides are ready to create it. It follows that rejection is not a verdict on your worth but a sign that a shared bubble didn't form: the other person wasn't ready to enter that space. It hurts, but it is not your failure as a person. Sloterdijk also reminds us of "thymos" — inner dignity. A refusal can wound it, but it doesn't depend on one other person's "no".
rejection.practice: Call someone in whose sphere you have long been welcome, and simply talk about anything. Notice: bubbles where you are awaited do exist.

abandonment.text: Sloterdijk offers an unexpected answer to why the fear of being abandoned lives in a person so deeply and for so long: it all began before the first breath. In the first volume of Spheres he writes that even before birth we have a first companion — the placenta, an organ we share, from which we are separated right at birth, before we even get to know it. In his view, people spend their whole lives looking for a substitute for this first "other", creating bubbles of closeness. If we follow his thought further, the fear of being left is very ancient — almost prehistoric for each of us. It doesn't speak of your weakness. But it doesn't predict the future either. You can notice that you have already created new connections many times.
abandonment.practice: Walk in your mind through the years of your life and pause at three people with whom you shared a warm sphere. Tell yourself: "I know how to build closeness — I have done it more than once."

unrequited.text: Plato's Eros is the child of Poverty, forever lacking something; Sloterdijk asks us not to forget that the soul also has another, giving side. Unrequited love combines the strength of a feeling with its impossibility — and that is exhausting. In Rage and Time he argues against the way modern culture sees the human being mainly through "eros" — desire that always lacks something. He reminds us of another side of the soul — "thymos": pride, dignity, generosity, the capacity to give. Sloterdijk would probably say that in unrequited love eros is left alone, without support: you are entirely in lack. Sloterdijk would suggest remembering thymos: your capacity to love is also your generosity and strength, not only a wound. Leaning on your dignity, you can respect your feeling without letting it determine your worth.
unrequited.practice: Send some of your generosity where it will be received: today give a small gift, a compliment or a favour to someone who will be glad of it. Thymos loves to give.

humiliation.text: The Greeks called "thymos" the inner heat that rises when someone tries to make you smaller. Humiliation wounds deeply, and this pain deserves respect. In Rage and Time, Sloterdijk places at the centre "thymos" — the sense of one's own dignity, which demands recognition. Humiliation is a direct blow to thymos, and it's natural that anger, shame and the wish to defend yourself rise in response. Sloterdijk believes these feelings shouldn't be suppressed: they show that dignity is alive. And in Critique of Cynical Reason he recalls Diogenes, who answered the arrogance of the powerful with bodily, cheerful impudence. In other words, humiliation says more about those who humiliated than about you. Your dignity is wounded, but not cancelled.
humiliation.practice: Straighten your back, plant your feet firmly and tell yourself: "My dignity is still with me." Stand like this for a minute, feeling the ground beneath you.

body_shame.text: Diogenes warmed himself in the sun in the middle of the square and lived in his body without shame, with cheerful freedom — Sloterdijk loves this image. Dissatisfaction with one's body is almost everywhere today, and there's no need to blame yourself for it. Sloterdijk sees the human being as a creature of exercise: we have always worked on ourselves — body, mind, habits. He calls this "anthropotechnics". But he also shows that practice can turn into a whip when "vertical tension" — the pull towards an ideal — becomes a constant reproach. Modern culture offers the body an endless series of unattainable ideals. For Sloterdijk, dissatisfaction with your body is a vertical that has stopped inspiring and started to press down. The body is not only a project to be improved but also a home you live in.
body_shame.practice: Move for a minute just for pleasure, like Diogenes in the sun: stretch, roll your shoulders, sway your hips. Don't judge the shape — just feel.

illness.text: Nietzsche wrote his books between migraine attacks, nearly blind, in cheap boarding houses — and Sloterdijk admires this art of living. Illness takes away strength and familiar possibilities, and you have every right to be angry, sad and tired. In You Must Change Your Life he writes a great deal about Nietzsche, who was ill for almost his entire life and still found ways to live and think — in the preface to The Gay Science, Nietzsche called his book the gratitude of a convalescent. Sloterdijk sees the human being as a creature able to adapt by creating new exercises for new circumstances. Then illness changes which "exercises of life" are available to you, but it doesn't cancel the very capacity to practise. This is not a call to heroism. Sometimes the exercise is simply to rest, to accept help, or to notice one good moment in the day.
illness.practice: Find an exercise that fits your present strength: five slow out-breaths, or a minute at the window looking at the sky. Today that is enough.

pride.text: An Olympic champion on the podium doesn't lower their eyes — and Sloterdijk thinks you needn't either. Pride in what you have done is a good, deserved feeling. Sloterdijk gives it a special place. In Rage and Time he says that modern culture has become too absorbed in "eros" — desire and lack — and has underestimated "thymos": pride, dignity, joy in one's own strength. For Sloterdijk, thymos is not a vice but a necessary part of a healthy soul. And in You Must Change Your Life he shows that the human being is a creature of exercise: every achievement is the fruit of repetition and effort. Through this lens, healthy pride is a fair recognition of your training. There's no need to hide it or be ashamed of it. Let yourself enjoy this feeling: it feeds your strength for the next exercises.
pride.practice: Stand as if on a podium: shoulders back, chin slightly up — and silently count how many repetitions lay behind this result. Tell yourself: "I trained for this."

melancholy.text: A soap bubble shimmers most beautifully in the last seconds before it bursts. Gentle sadness is a quiet feeling that doesn't need fixing. Sloterdijk opens the first volume of Spheres with the image of a child blowing soap bubbles. The child watches with delight as a bubble floats through the air, as if carrying on the child's own breath — until it bursts. For Sloterdijk, this is an image of all human spaces of closeness: they are beautiful and fragile at once. It follows that gentle sadness is the feeling of someone who sees both the beauty of the bubble and its brevity. There is no despair in it: bubbles burst, but people blow them again and again. Melancholy lets you value what is here now precisely because it is not eternal.
melancholy.practice: Blow a soap bubble — or simply imagine one — and follow it with your eyes until it bursts. Then recall a recent beautiful moment that has also already passed.
